target: Es algo de lo que no me gusta hablar.
english: It's something I don't like to talk about.
tip: "De lo que" = about which (abstract): "De lo que hablamos" = What we talked about. Neuter lo for ideas, not physical objects.

target: Estoy decepcionado de que no hayas cumplido tu promesa.
english: I am disappointed that you didn't keep your promise.
tip: Decepcionado looks like deceived but means disappointed – nobody lied, they just let you down. Actual deception is engaño; decepción is dashed hopes.

target: La mujer cuyo hijo estudia conmigo es abogada.
english: The woman whose son studies with me is a lawyer.
tip: Cuyo hijo, not cuya, after la mujer: cuyo agrees with the thing owned (hijo), never the owner. English whose never budges; Spanish whose bends to what follows.

target: Me han dado un plantón.
english: I was stood up.
tip: A 'plantón' is literally a big sapling – planted and left standing. 'Me han dado un plantón' = they planted you like a tree and walked off: stood up.

target: Les pedí que vinieran temprano.
english: I asked them to come early.
tip: English asks people TO do things; Spanish can't. 'Les pedí que vinieran' – after pedir you need a full que-clause, never an infinitive for another person.

target: He perdido las llaves otra vez.
english: I've lost my keys again.
tip: 'He perdido' today – in Spain. Spaniards use the perfect for anything from today; most of Latin America says 'perdí' even for five minutes ago. Both are correct.

target: Mi hijo ha aprobado el examen.
english: My son has passed the exam.
tip: 'Ha aprobado' isn't 'has approved' – aprobar un examen means to PASS it. The examiner approves your answers, so YOU 'aprobar' the exam.

target: Se habrá olvidado de la reunión.
english: He must have forgotten about the meeting.
tip: 'Habrá olvidado' isn't a prediction – future tenses double as guesses about the present. 'Se habrá olvidado' = he MUST have forgotten.

target: Por cierto, ¿has visto mi cargador?
english: By the way, have you seen my charger?
tip: Trap: cierto means 'true,' yet por cierto isn't 'for certain' – it signals a topic swerve, 'by the way.' To actually say 'certainly,' you'd want sin duda.

target: Ojalá hubiera más tiempo para descansar.
english: I wish there were more time to rest.
tip: 'Ojalá' comes from Arabic 'law sha'a Allah', if God wills – a holdover from Moorish Spain, hence the subjunctive 'hubiera' in every wish.

target: Hemos vuelto a cometer el mismo error.
english: We've made the same mistake again.
tip: 'Hemos vuelto a cometer' isn't about returning anywhere. Volver a + infinitive = do it AGAIN – Spanish 're-does' actions by 'returning to' them.

target: La casa donde crecí la han derribado.
english: The house where I grew up has been torn down.
tip: Why the extra 'la'? When the object moves up front – 'La casa... LA han derribado' – Spanish must echo it with a pronoun. English fronts silently; Spanish leaves a marker.

target: Como si fuera la primera vez que lo hace.
english: As if it were the first time he did it.
tip: 'Como si' always takes past subjunctive – 'como si fuera' – even when English happily says 'as if it IS'. No exceptions.

target: Si tuviera más dinero, viajaría por todo el mundo.
english: If I had more money, I would travel around the world.
tip: Never 'si tendría'! After si, Spanish bans the conditional: 'si tuviera... viajaría'. The -ra form belongs in the if-half, -ría in the result.

target: Todavía no he decidido si aceptaré la oferta de trabajo.
english: I still haven't decided whether I will accept the job offer.
tip: Wait – future after si? 'Si aceptaré' is legal because this si means 'whether', not 'if'. Only condition-si bans the future; whether-si allows any tense.

target: Es increíble que ya hayan pasado diez años desde la boda.
english: It's incredible that ten years have already passed since the wedding.
tip: Ten years HAVE passed – pure fact. But hayan pasado goes subjunctive anyway: es increíble que filters the fact through your amazement, and feelings trigger subjunctive.

target: Nunca he visto nada igual.
english: I've never seen anything like it.
tip: 'Nunca... nada' – a double negative, and it's mandatory. Spanish negatives must agree: once nunca opens the sentence, 'anything' becomes 'nada', never 'algo'.

target: Ha sido un placer hablar contigo.
english: It's been a pleasure talking to you.
tip: Contigo is a Latin fossil: tecum meant 'you-with,' Spanish bolted con onto the front, and the old cum melted into the final -go. Conmigo hides the same relic.

target: Insistió en que nos quedáramos a cenar.
english: She insisted we stay for dinner.
tip: English drops the 'on' in 'insisted (on) that...'; Spanish never does: 'insistió EN que'. Verbs keep their preposition even before a whole que-clause.

target: Esperaba que me llamaran para la entrevista.
english: I was hoping they would call me for the interview.
tip: 'Esperaba' is three English verbs at once: hope, wait, expect. 'Esperaba que me llamaran' = I hoped they'd call – context, not the verb, tells you which.

target: Tan pronto como crucemos la frontera, cambiaremos dinero.
english: As soon as we cross the border, we'll exchange money.
tip: 'Tan pronto como crucemos' – not cruzamos. Time clauses about the future take subjunctive; English hides the not-yet-real behind plain present ('as soon as we cross').

target: Habíamos quedado a las ocho, pero no vino.
english: We had agreed to meet at eight, but he didn't come.
tip: 'Habíamos quedado' isn't about staying. Plain quedar = arrange to meet ('we'd agreed on eight'); quedarse, with the reflexive, = stay.

target: Habré terminado de hacer las maletas para las diez.
english: I will have finished packing by ten.
tip: The deadline word is para: para las diez means 'BY ten,' a finish line. Habré terminado plus para is how Spanish promises something done before a set time.

target: De ahí que la familia decidiera mudarse al campo.
english: That's why the family decided to move to the countryside.
tip: 'De ahí que' – literally 'from there that' – means 'that's why', yet oddly demands subjunctive: 'decidiera'. The result is real, but the formula is fixed.

target: De haber tenido más tiempo, habríamos explorado la selva.
english: Had we had more time, we would have explored the jungle.
tip: "De haber + participle" is a formal alternative to "si hubiéramos + participle" for past unreal conditions.

target: Si hubiera invertido en esa empresa, ahora sería rico.
english: If I had invested in that company, I would be rich now.
tip: 'hubiera invertido' is the past unrealized condition; 'sería' gives the present hypothetical result – a mixed conditional.

target: Si bien el hotel era caro, la ubicación lo compensaba.
english: Although the hotel was expensive, the location made up for it.
tip: 'Si bien' isn't 'if well' – it's a formal 'although', and unlike conditional si it takes plain indicative: 'si bien el hotel era caro'. No hypothesis in sight.

target: No solo subieron los precios, sino que también redujeron la calidad.
english: Not only did they raise prices, but they also reduced quality.
tip: English has one 'but'; Spanish splits it. After a negative like no solo, it must be sino, never pero – pero contradicts, sino replaces or piles on. Here it stacks a second complaint.

target: Se ha demostrado que esta técnica funciona.
english: It has been demonstrated that this technique works.
tip: "Se ha demostrado" = It has been shown. Impersonal se works in all tenses: "Se ha dicho que..." = It has been said that...

target: Confío en que el equipo logrará superar las expectativas.
english: I trust that the team will manage to exceed expectations.
tip: 'Confío en que' + indicative 'logrará': trust asserts rather than doubts, so no subjunctive needed – unlike 'dudo que', which always flips it.
